Over 600 autonomous rocket landings so far


X Freeze (@XFreeze)

Most people don’t realize how insanely autonomous Falcon 9 already is

Once Falcon 9 lifts off, almost the entire mission is executed by the rocket itself

And the crazy part is

This autonomy does not depend on generative AI

It comes from brutally refined flight software, physics, sensors, control theory and advanced optimization.....improved across hundreds of missions

Falcon 9 autonomously handles:

→ Liftoff and ascent through closed-loop guidance
→ Stage separation at precisely calculated conditions
→ Engine ignition and shutdown sequences
→ Orbital insertion and payload deployment
→ Booster boostback, entry and landing burns
→ Real-time guidance corrections during descent
→ Landing on a floating droneship hundreds of kilometers offshore
→ Autonomous flight termination if mission safety rules are violated

A 70-meter orbital rocket launches itself, separates itself, puts a payload into orbit.....then the first stage falls back through the atmosphere and lands itself on a floating platform hundreds of kilometers offshore

Physics, software, and hardware engineered to absurd precision

Falcon 9 is one of the greatest autonomous machines humanity has ever built

And SpaceX made it look routine

Kevin Dahlstrom (@Camp4)

Most people have no idea how far ahead Tesla is, because the cars look and drive like other cars.

But under the hood, Teslas bear little resemblance to other cars. Every component is (or will be) re-thought from first principles.

Even if legacy automakers had the will to start from scratch (they don’t), they don’t have the capability.

One example:

Ford relies on 150 separate vendors just for its software. Codebases don’t integrate and Ford has to get supplier permission for modifications. Just unwinding that mess will take years.

I recently bought a new Toyota for my daughter and it was like stepping back in time. Everything from the buying process to the car itself is largely the same as it was fifty years ago. It’s only improved incrementally.

Tesla has built a massive technology lead and—equally importantly—has superior economics.

Cybercab is the first example of Tesla leveraging that dominance, but it’s still early days.

• Fixed mid-turn UI freezes when the terminal stops reading output.
• Fixed crashes that occurred when the terminal pane was closed while grok was exiting.
• MCP server list in minimal mode now correctly shows policy-blocked servers.
• URLs that wrap across multiple lines inside quotes or lists are now fully clickable.
• The welcome screen composer now grows taller when you paste multi-line text.
• Enterprise policy files are no longer deleted on startup when your team login is stored at a custom `GROK_AUTH_PATH`.
• /feedback now drops unsupported images with a notice (matching the modal) and never loses your report text on save errors.
• Feedback drafts keep their paragraph breaks when updated, and the modal no longer switches tabs unexpectedly.
• Turn summary lines no longer lose their spacing after background tasks finish.
• Thinking blocks no longer stay expanded after switching between fullscreen and minimal modes.

Performance:
• First prompt after login is faster when MCP servers are configured; they connect in the background.

I had the chance to talk to the head of the Reaction Injection Molding (RIM) Tesla team that developed the process, machines, materials and production line responsible for the Cybercab exterior (and some interior) plastic panels.

What is RIM? Reaction injection molding (RIM) is a manufacturing process that injects two liquid chemicals into a mold to create strong, lightweight plastic parts.

The primary benefits to Tesla? Tesla uses Reaction Injection Molding (RIM) for the Cybercab primarily to eliminate the traditional automotive paint shop, which is historically one of the most expensive, space-consuming, and environmentally taxing parts of car manufacturing. Tesla's goal for mass production is a highly compact, parallel modular assembly system called the "unboxed" process.

By skipping the massive infrastructure of a paint shop, Tesla can reduce the factory footprint by roughly 50%. Since the colored panels come out of the molds nearly complete, they don't have to follow a strict sequential painting order and can be easily bolted on toward the end of assembly, minimizing the risk of factory scratches.

In the Tesla application for Cybercab, the RIM gold exterior body panels have a underlying reinforced plastic inner support panel that is plastic laser welded (& some industrial adhesives) bonded to the outer panel.

When I first saw the early production tests, I noticed there were visible "distortions" where the contact points occurred and this detracted from the overall look of the Cybercab. 

The team worked very hard to address this issue and made a number of production process modifications that virtually eliminated this issue and I can say the Cybercabs I saw and rode in at the Launch Event looked exceptionally clean. 

Amazing work by the Plastics team to not only develop this process and the machinery and materials used, but to refine the production process to get such an amazing result!
